people.short_bio: A Roman monk who became pope in 672. He is remembered for care of monasteries and for opposing the Monothelite teaching.
people.long_bio: Adeodatus was a monk of the monastery of St Erasmus on the Caelian Hill in Rome before his election. As pope he worked to strengthen monastic discipline and, like his predecessors, resisted Monothelitism. Only two of his letters survive, granting privileges to the abbeys of St Peter at Canterbury and St Martin at Tours.

people.long_bio: Donus was a Roman, the son of Mauricius. In a short reign he paved the atrium before St Peter's with marble and restored churches. Archbishop Reparatus of Ravenna submitted to the Holy See, ending Ravenna's attempt at independence, and Donus dispersed a community of Nestorian monks in Rome, giving their house to Roman monks.

people.long_bio: Agatho came from Sicily and may have been a monk before joining the Roman clergy; an old tradition says he was very elderly when elected. He held a Lateran synod that restored St Wilfrid to the see of York, and sent legates and a doctrinal letter to the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which condemned Monothelitism. He died before its decrees reached Rome.

people.short_bio: A Sicilian, son of Paul, elected in 681 but consecrated only in 682 after imperial approval. He confirmed and spread the decrees of the Sixth Ecumenical Council.
people.long_bio: Leo II was a Sicilian, the son of a man named Paul. His consecration waited many months for the emperor's confirmation. He accepted the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which also condemned his predecessor Honorius I, and sent them to the churches of the West, including Spain. He ended the special independence of the archbishops of Ravenna and moved relics of martyrs from the catacombs into a church in Rome.

people.short_bio: A Roman trained in the papal choir school, pope from 684 to 685. He won from the emperor a relaxation of imperial control over papal elections.
people.long_bio: Benedict, son of John, was trained from youth in the Roman schola cantorum and known for his knowledge of Scripture, his singing and his care for the poor. He waited almost a year for imperial confirmation of his election. Emperor Constantine IV then decreed that such confirmation would no longer be needed from Constantinople, or could be given by the exarch in Italy. He worked to win Spanish acceptance of the Sixth Council and restored many Roman churches.

people.short_bio: A Syrian from the region of Antioch, the first of a series of Eastern popes. He had represented Rome at the Sixth Ecumenical Council.
people.long_bio: John, son of Cyriacus, came from the province of Antioch. As a deacon he was one of the papal representatives at the Sixth Ecumenical Council and brought its acts back to Rome in 682. Elected in 685 without waiting for imperial confirmation, he reigned only a year, much of it ill, but was remembered for his generosity to the clergy and the poor and for securing tax relief on papal estates in Sicily and Calabria.

people.context: Refugees from the Arab conquests of Syria and Palestine had settled in Rome and Sicily, and Greek-speaking clergy were prominent. A run of popes of Eastern origin began with John V.

people.short_bio: A compromise candidate elected in 686, already elderly. He grew up in Sicily, and his origins are unknown.
people.long_bio: Conon was the son of an officer of the Thracesian regiment of the imperial army and was educated in Sicily before becoming a priest in Rome. When clergy and soldiers deadlocked over rival candidates, he was chosen as a compromise. Old and ill, he reigned less than a year. He consecrated the Irish missionary St Kilian and sent him to preach in Franconia, and received tax concessions from Emperor Justinian II.
actions: Consecrated St Kilian for the mission to Franconia

people.context: In Rome the clergy, the army and the people competed over papal elections, which still needed the exarch's confirmation at Ravenna.

birthplace.public_note: His family was Syrian, from the region of Antioch, but he was born in Palermo.

people.short_bio: Born in Palermo to a Syrian family, pope from 687 to 701. He refused to accept the Council in Trullo and is credited with adding the Agnus Dei to the Mass.
people.long_bio: Sergius, son of Tiberius, was born in Palermo to a family from Antioch and came to Rome under Pope Adeodatus II. He was elected after a disputed contest in 687. He refused to sign the canons of the Council in Trullo (692), several of which criticised Roman practice; when Justinian II sent an officer to arrest him, the soldiers of Rome and Ravenna protected him. He baptised the West Saxon king Caedwalla, consecrated Willibrord for the Frisians, and added the Agnus Dei to the Mass.
actions: Rejected the canons of the Council in Trullo (692)
Consecrated Willibrord, apostle of the Frisians

Added the Agnus Dei to the Mass
Ended the Three Chapters schism at Aquileia
people.context: Rome remained under Byzantine rule, but Justinian II's attempt to force the Trullan canons on the pope failed because Italian troops sided with Sergius. Anglo-Saxon England and the Frankish lands looked increasingly to Rome.

people.short_bio: A Greek, pope from 701 to 705. He protected Rome's interests by mediation, calming mutinous troops and ransoming captives from the Lombards.
people.long_bio: John VI was Greek by birth. When Italian militias gathered against the exarch Theophylactus, he sent priests to calm them and avoided bloodshed. When the Lombard duke Gisulf of Benevento raided the Roman countryside, John sent priests with money to ransom captives and persuade him to withdraw. He also confirmed the rights of St Wilfrid of York.
actions: Averted violence between the exarch and Italian militias

people.context: Byzantine authority in Italy was weak, Italian militias were increasingly self-reliant, and the Lombard duchies pressed on Roman territory.

people.short_bio: A Greek, son of the official Plato, pope from 705 to 707. He is remembered for the frescoes of Santa Maria Antiqua.
people.long_bio: John VII, son of Plato and Blatta, came from a distinguished Greek family; he had been rector of the papal estates on the Appian Way. As pope he built a residence on the Palatine near Santa Maria Antiqua and adorned that church with frescoes that still survive, and built a chapel to Our Lady in St Peter's. Asked by Justinian II to approve the Trullan canons, he returned them without comment. He recovered papal estates in the Cottian Alps from the Lombard king Aripert II.

people.context: Byzantine culture was strong in Rome, where officials, clergy and monks from the East lived around the Palatine.

people.short_bio: A Syrian who reigned only about twenty days in 708. Badly crippled by gout, he still ordered repairs to Rome's walls.
people.long_bio: Sisinnius, son of John, was Syrian by birth. He was so crippled by gout that he could not feed himself, yet he was remembered as firm of character. In his three weeks as pope he ordered lime to be burnt for repairing the city walls and consecrated a bishop for Corsica.

people.short_bio: A Syrian, pope from 708 to 715, and the last pope to visit Constantinople until 1967. Justinian II received him with great honour.
people.long_bio: Constantine, son of John, came from a Syrian family. In 710 Justinian II summoned him to Constantinople to settle the dispute over the canons of the Council in Trullo. The emperor received him with honour and renewed the privileges of the Roman Church, and Constantine gave a qualified approval to the canons not against faith or morals. Soon after his return Justinian was overthrown, and the new emperor Philippicus favoured Monothelitism, which Rome rejected.

people.short_bio: A Roman who rose through the papal administration, pope from 715 to 731. He sent St Boniface to Germany and resisted the iconoclast emperor Leo III.
people.long_bio: Gregory, son of Marcellus and Honesta, served in the papal household as subdeacon, treasurer and librarian, and as deacon accompanied Pope Constantine to Constantinople. As pope he commissioned Boniface to preach in Germany and consecrated him bishop in 722. He opposed Emperor Leo III's heavy taxes and his edicts against holy images, while discouraging Italian revolt against the empire. His personal influence with the Lombard king Liutprand kept Rome safe.
actions: Sent St Boniface to Germany and consecrated him bishop (722)
Opposed Byzantine iconoclasm
Resisted imperial taxation
people.context: Emperor Leo III launched iconoclasm, the campaign against religious images. Italians resented Byzantine taxation, and the Lombard king Liutprand was expanding. The pope was becoming the real leader of Rome.

people.short_bio: A Syrian elected by acclaim in 731, the last pope to seek the Byzantine exarch's approval of his election. He condemned iconoclasm and asked the Franks for help against the Lombards.
people.long_bio: Gregory, son of John, was chosen by acclamation during his predecessor's funeral. He held synods in Rome in 731 that condemned the destruction of images, and publicly honoured images and relics. He supported Boniface's mission in Germany and sent Willibald to help him. Threatened by the Lombard king Liutprand, he appealed in 739 to the Frankish leader Charles Martel, a first step toward the papal alliance with the Franks.

Appealed to Charles Martel for help (739)

people.context: Iconoclasm divided Rome from Constantinople, and the emperor removed southern Italy and Illyricum from papal jurisdiction. The Lombards threatened Rome, and the Franks were emerging as a possible protector.

people.short_bio: The last pope of Greek origin, from 741 to 752. A skilled diplomat, he won peace from the Lombards and approved Pepin's kingship.
people.long_bio: Zachary, son of Polychronius, was of Greek origin. He went in person to the Lombard king Liutprand and secured the return of four cities and a twenty-year truce, and later talked him out of attacking Ravenna. When the Frankish mayor Pepin asked whether a powerless king should keep the title, Zachary's answer backed Pepin becoming king in 751. He worked closely with Boniface, and translated Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Greek.

Supported Pepin's elevation as king of the Franks (751)

people.context: Byzantine power in Italy was collapsing; the Lombards were close to taking Ravenna. In Francia the Carolingian family replaced the Merovingian kings with papal approval.

people.short_bio: A Roman, pope from 752 to 757. He crossed the Alps to seek Frankish help, and the lands Pepin gave him became the start of the Papal States.
people.long_bio: Stephen was elected in 752 after the death after a few days of a priest also called Stephen, which is why he is sometimes counted as Stephen III. Faced with the Lombard king Aistulf, who had taken Ravenna and threatened Rome, he travelled to Francia in 753-754, anointed Pepin and his sons, and received Pepin's promise to restore the lost territories. After Pepin's campaigns, the exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis were handed to the pope.
actions: Travelled to Francia and anointed Pepin as king (754)
Received the Donation of Pepin (756)
Became in effect the first ruler of the Papal States

people.context: With Ravenna fallen to the Lombards (751) and no help from Constantinople, the papacy turned to the Franks. This alliance created the Papal States and reshaped Western Europe.
people.public_uncertainty: His numbering varies (II or III) because of an elected priest who died before consecration.

people.short_bio: A Roman, brother and successor of Stephen II, pope from 757 to 767. He kept up the Frankish alliance and moved relics from the ruined catacombs into city churches.
people.long_bio: Paul, brother of Stephen II, was educated at the Lateran and served his brother in church affairs. As pope he kept close ties with Pepin, pressed the Lombard king Desiderius to give back seized towns, and opposed the iconoclast emperor Constantine V. He founded San Silvestro in Capite and moved many martyrs' relics from the damaged catacombs into Roman churches, including those of St Petronilla to St Peter's.

people.context: The new Papal State had to defend itself against the Lombard king Desiderius and against Byzantine claims, relying on Frankish support.

people.short_bio: A Sicilian Benedictine monk, pope from 768 to 772. His Lateran synod of 769 barred laymen from election as pope.
people.long_bio: Stephen, son of Olivus, was born in Sicily about 720 and came to Rome young. He was a monk, and Pope Zachary ordained him priest. He was elected after the lay antipope Constantine was overthrown, though he could not prevent the brutal treatment of the deposed. The Lateran synod of 769 ruled that only clergy could be elected pope, and condemned iconoclasm. Later the Lombard king Desiderius manipulated papal politics through Stephen's chamberlain.
actions: Lateran synod of 769 excluded laymen from papal elections
Condemned the antipope Constantine II
Reaffirmed the veneration of images
people.context: Roman aristocratic factions fought over the papacy, which now ruled territory. The Lombard king Desiderius tried to win over the Franks through marriage to Charlemagne.

people.short_bio: A Roman noble, pope for almost 24 years (772-795). Allied with Charlemagne, who ended the Lombard kingdom, he presided by legates over the Second Council of Nicaea.
people.long_bio: Adrian came from a noble Roman family and served under Paul I and Stephen III. When the Lombard king Desiderius threatened Rome, he called on Charlemagne, who conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774 and, visiting Rome at Easter, confirmed and enlarged the papal territories. His legates took part in the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which approved the veneration of images. He also opposed Adoptionism and improved Rome's walls, churches and aqueducts. Charlemagne wrote his epitaph.
actions: Allied with Charlemagne, who ended the Lombard kingdom (774)
Confirmed and enlarged papal territory
Approved the Second Council of Nicaea (787)
Opposed Adoptionism
Restored Rome's walls and aqueducts
people.context: Charlemagne built a vast Frankish realm. The papacy now relied on him rather than on Constantinople, while in the East the Empress Irene ended the first phase of iconoclasm.

saint.public_note: His name was added to the Roman Martyrology in 1673.

people.short_bio: A Roman priest elected in 795, who crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800. He survived a violent attack by Roman nobles in 799.
people.long_bio: Leo, son of Atyuppius and Elizabeth, was cardinal-priest of Santa Susanna and probably head of the papal treasury. In April 799 relatives of his predecessor attacked him during a procession, trying to blind him and cut out his tongue; he escaped and fled to Charlemagne at Paderborn. Restored to Rome, he cleared himself by oath, and on Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's, placed the imperial crown on Charlemagne's head. He refused to add the Filioque to the Creed, though he accepted its teaching.
actions: Crowned Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's, 25 December 800
Survived the attack of 799 and took refuge with Charlemagne at Paderborn

people.context: The coronation of 800 revived a Western emperor alongside the Byzantine one, where the Empress Irene ruled. It tied the papacy to the Carolingians and set the pattern of the medieval empire.

people.short_bio: A Roman noble who reigned only seven months (816-817). He went to Francia and crowned Louis the Pious emperor.
people.long_bio: Stephen, son of Marinus, came from a noble Roman family and was ordained deacon by Leo III. Immediately after his election he had the Romans swear loyalty to Emperor Louis the Pious, and then travelled to Francia, where he crowned and anointed Louis at Reims in 816, renewing the papal-Frankish alliance. He died soon after his return.

people.context: The Carolingian empire dominated the West, and popes and emperors negotiated how much control the emperor had over Rome and papal elections. Roman noble families competed for the papacy.

people.short_bio: A Roman, pope from 817 to 824. He received the Pactum Ludovicianum from Louis the Pious and rebuilt Santa Prassede and Santa Cecilia, with mosaics that survive.
people.long_bio: Paschal, son of Bonosus, grew up in the Lateran and was head of the monastery of St Stephen near St Peter's, caring for pilgrims. As pope he received from Louis the Pious the Pactum Ludovicianum confirming papal rights and lands, and crowned Lothair I in 823. He supported missions to the north and Theodore the Studite against Byzantine iconoclasm. He rebuilt Santa Prassede, Santa Cecilia and Santa Maria in Domnica, whose mosaics show him with a square halo, and moved St Cecilia's relics to Trastevere.

people.long_bio: Eugene was archpriest of Santa Sabina on the Aventine when elected with the support of the nobility. In 824 he agreed to the Constitutio Romana with Lothair, acting for Louis the Pious, which strengthened imperial oversight in Rome and required a new pope to swear loyalty before consecration. His Roman council of 826 issued disciplinary decrees, including a call for schools at cathedrals and churches.

people.short_bio: A Roman from the Via Lata district who reigned only about forty days in 827.
people.long_bio: Valentine entered the service of the church young. Paschal I ordained him and made him archdeacon, an office he kept under Eugene II. Elected in 827, he died about a month or forty days later, and little else is known of his reign.
people.context: The Carolingian empire dominated the West, and popes and emperors negotiated how much control the emperor had over Rome and papal elections. Roman noble families competed for the papacy.

people.short_bio: A Roman, pope from 827 to 844. He was drawn into the wars between Louis the Pious and his sons, and fortified Ostia against Saracen raids.
people.long_bio: Gregory, son of John, was cardinal-priest of San Marco. His consecration waited for imperial approval until 828. In 833 he went with Lothair to Francia, hoping to make peace between Louis the Pious and his sons, but Louis was deposed and Gregory's credibility suffered. He built the fortress of Gregoriopolis at Ostia against the Saracens, repaired aqueducts, made Ansgar papal legate to the North and encouraged the feast of All Saints across the empire.
actions: Intervened in the conflict between Louis the Pious and his sons (833)
Fortified Ostia (Gregoriopolis)
Named Ansgar legate for Scandinavia
Promoted the feast of All Saints
people.context: The Carolingian empire dominated the West, and popes and emperors negotiated how much control the emperor had over Rome and papal elections. Roman noble families competed for the papacy. Saracens conquered much of Sicily in these years.

people.short_bio: A Roman noble, pope from 844 to 847. During his reign Saracen raiders sacked St Peter's and St Paul's outside the walls.
people.long_bio: Sergius came from a noble Roman family and was archpriest under Gregory IV. His election in 844 was contested by the deacon John, who was set aside. He was consecrated without waiting for the emperor, and Lothair sent his son Louis to Rome to investigate; Sergius crowned Louis king of the Lombards. In 846 Saracens plundered the basilicas of St Peter and St Paul outside the walls. His brother Benedict was accused of simony, though the reports may be exaggerated.
actions: Crowned Louis II king of the Lombards (844)
Named Drogo of Metz papal vicar in Francia
Restored the Lateran basilica

people.short_bio: A Roman, pope from 847 to 855. He built the Leonine Wall around the Vatican after the Saracen raid of 846.
people.long_bio: Leo, son of Radoald, was educated at the monastery of St Martin near St Peter's and became cardinal-priest of the Santi Quattro Coronati. Elected in 847 amid fear of the Saracens, he was consecrated without waiting for the emperor. He enclosed the Vatican with a wall, creating the Leonine City (852), and joined Naples, Amalfi and Gaeta in the naval victory at Ostia in 849. In 853 he received the young Alfred of Wessex. He also condemned the ambitious cardinal Anastasius.
actions: Built the Leonine Wall around the Vatican (completed 852)
Joined the alliance that defeated the Saracens off Ostia (849)
Received the young Alfred of Wessex (853)
Restored churches damaged in 846
people.context: After the Carolingian empire broke apart, rival Italian and German claimants fought for the imperial crown, and Roman factions fought for the papacy. Saracen raiders threatened the coasts of Italy.
open_questions: Roster consecration date 10.V.847 differs from 10.IV.847 in the Vatican Italian table and CE.

people.short_bio: A learned Roman, son of Peter, pope from 855 to 858. He overcame the imperially backed antipope Anastasius.
people.long_bio: Benedict, son of Peter, was elected after Leo IV's death, but the imperial envoys backed the excommunicated cardinal Anastasius, who seized the Lateran and imprisoned Benedict. The Roman clergy and people stayed loyal, and Benedict was consecrated in September 855; he later admitted Anastasius to lay communion. He received King Aethelwulf of Wessex and his son Alfred, and repaired churches damaged by the Saracens. A coin of his reign is cited against the legend of 'Pope Joan'.
actions: Overcame the antipope Anastasius (855)
Received King Aethelwulf of Wessex and Alfred
Repaired Roman churches damaged in 846
people.context: After the Carolingian empire broke apart, rival Italian and German claimants fought for the imperial crown, and Roman factions fought for the papacy. Saracen raiders threatened the coasts of Italy.

saint.note: S. in Vatican table; Vatican News lists St Nicholas I on 13 November. CE: regarded as a saint after death, no formal canonization date.

people.short_bio: A Roman, pope from 858 to 867, often called the Great. He asserted papal authority over bishops and kings, and clashed with Patriarch Photius.
people.long_bio: Nicholas, son of the papal official Theodore, served Sergius II, Leo IV and Benedict III. As pope he refused to recognise Photius, who had replaced the deposed patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, and excommunicated him in 863. He would not allow King Lothair II to abandon his wife Theutberga, upheld appeals to Rome against Archbishop Hincmar of Reims and disciplined Archbishop John of Ravenna. His answers to the questions of the newly baptised Bulgarian ruler Boris are a famous pastoral document.
actions: Refused to recognise Photius as patriarch (863)
Defended Queen Theutberga against Lothair II's divorce
Upheld the right of bishops to appeal to Rome
Answered the questions of the Bulgarian ruler Boris (866)
people.context: The Carolingian realms were divided among quarrelling kings, while Constantinople, newly confident, competed with Rome for the conversion of the Bulgarians and Slavs. The Photian dispute was an early sign of the East-West estrangement.

people.short_bio: An elderly Roman, once married, pope from 867 to 872. He supported Cyril and Methodius and approved the Slavonic liturgy.
people.long_bio: Adrian came from the Roman family that had produced Stephen IV and Sergius II, and had been married before ordination. Elected when already old, he kept peace among Charlemagne's heirs and admitted Lothair II to communion on his oath to take back his lawful wife. His legates presided at the council of Constantinople in 869-870, which deposed Photius. He welcomed Cyril and Methodius to Rome and approved the liturgy in Slavonic. His later years were saddened by a family tragedy.
actions: Approved the Slavonic liturgy of Cyril and Methodius
Presided by legates at the council of Constantinople (869-870)
Admitted Lothair II to communion on oath
people.context: After the Carolingian empire broke apart, rival Italian and German claimants fought for the imperial crown, and Roman factions fought for the papacy. Saracen raiders threatened the coasts of Italy.

people.short_bio: A Roman archdeacon, pope from 872 to 882. He crowned two emperors and fought the Saracens himself, and is often said to have been murdered.
people.long_bio: John, son of Gundus, had long served as archdeacon. As pope he crowned Charles the Bald emperor in 875 and Charles the Fat in 881, looking for a protector against the Saracens. He fortified St Paul's outside the walls, defeated a Saracen fleet off Circeo in 876 and even paid tribute to raiders. He restored Methodius to Moravia and allowed the Slavonic liturgy, and opposed Formosus, Bishop of Porto, whom he excommunicated. According to the Annals of Fulda he was killed by a relative, but historians are divided.
actions: Crowned Charles the Bald (875) and Charles the Fat (881) as emperors
Defeated a Saracen fleet off Circeo (876)
Supported Methodius and the Slavonic liturgy
Excommunicated Formosus and his party (876)
people.context: After the Carolingian empire broke apart, rival Italian and German claimants fought for the imperial crown, and Roman factions fought for the papacy. Saracen raiders threatened the coasts of Italy.
people.public_uncertainty: The story that he was murdered comes from a single chronicle and is disputed.

people.short_bio: Born at Gallese, north of Rome, pope from 882 to 884. Already Bishop of Caere, he was one of the first bishops to move to the see of Rome.
people.long_bio: Marinus, son of the priest Palumbo, entered the Roman church at twelve. He served on three embassies to Constantinople, including as legate at the council of 869-870, and was once imprisoned there. John VIII made him Bishop of Caere (Cerveteri), treasurer and archdeacon. As pope he restored Formosus to his see, renewed the condemnation of Photius, and at King Alfred's request freed the English quarter in Rome from taxes. Some chroniclers wrongly called him Martin II.
actions: Restored Formosus to the see of Porto
Renewed the condemnation of Photius
Freed the English Schola in Rome from taxes at Alfred's request

saint.public_note: His long-standing local cult was officially confirmed in 1891.

people.short_bio: A Roman who reigned just over a year (884-885). He died near Modena on his way to Germany and was buried at Nonantola, where he was venerated.
people.long_bio: Adrian, son of Benedict, was elected in 884 amid violent Roman factional struggles. Sources record harsh punishments: he had the official George of the Aventine blinded and a noblewoman named Maria flogged through the city. In 885 he set out to meet Emperor Charles the Fat about the imperial succession, but died at San Cesario sul Panaro near Modena. He was buried at the abbey of Nonantola, where a cult grew up.
actions: Set out to settle the imperial succession with Charles the Fat
Venerated at Nonantola after his death
people.context: After the Carolingian empire broke apart, rival Italian and German claimants fought for the imperial crown, and Roman factions fought for the papacy. Saracen raiders threatened the coasts of Italy.
people.public_uncertainty: Some sources suggest his death was a revenge killing, but this is not proven.
open_questions: Feast date varies by source: 8 July (Treccani) vs 7 September (CE).

people.short_bio: A Roman aristocrat, pope from 885 to 891. He used his family's wealth to relieve famine and crowned Guy of Spoleto emperor.
people.long_bio: Stephen, son of the noble Hadrian, was brought up by his relative Bishop Zachary, librarian of the Holy See, and was cardinal-priest of the Santi Quattro Coronati. He was consecrated without waiting for imperial approval. Finding the papal treasury empty in a time of famine, he used his father's wealth to feed the poor and ransom captives. He adopted Guy of Spoleto as his son and crowned him emperor in 891, and resisted Photius.
actions: Relieved famine in Rome from family wealth
Crowned Guy of Spoleto emperor (891)
Recognised Louis the Blind as king of Provence

people.short_bio: Bishop of Porto who became pope in 891, probably Roman-born. After his death his corpse was put on trial in the notorious Cadaver Synod.
people.long_bio: Formosus, born about 816 and probably a Roman, became Bishop of Porto in 864 and led a papal mission to Bulgaria. In 876 John VIII excommunicated him, but Marinus I restored him. As pope he crowned Guy of Spoleto's son Lambert, then invited the East Frankish king Arnulf to Italy and crowned him emperor in 896. Months after his death, Stephen VI had his body exhumed, judged in the Cadaver Synod (897) and thrown into the Tiber. Later popes rehabilitated him and he was reburied in St Peter's.
actions: Papal legate to Bulgaria (866-867)
Crowned Lambert of Spoleto co-emperor (892)
Crowned Arnulf of Carinthia emperor (896)
Posthumously tried in the Cadaver Synod (897) and later rehabilitated
people.context: After the Carolingian empire broke apart, rival Italian and German claimants fought for the imperial crown, and Roman factions fought for the papacy. Saracen raiders threatened the coasts of Italy. The rivalry between the Spoletan party and Arnulf's supporters made Formosus's memory a political battleground.
people.public_uncertainty: His birth in Rome is probable rather than certain.

people.short_bio: A Roman who reigned about fifteen days in April 896. He had earlier been twice deprived of holy orders.
people.long_bio: Boniface had been deposed from orders twice, once as subdeacon and once as priest, yet was elected by a Roman faction after Formosus died. He reigned about fifteen days; some sources say he died of gout, others that he was forced out to make way for Stephen VI. A synod under John IX in 898 declared his election null.

people.short_bio: A Roman, pope from 896 to 897, remembered for the Cadaver Synod against Formosus. He was later imprisoned and strangled.
people.long_bio: Stephen, son of the priest John, had been made Bishop of Anagni by Formosus. Backed by the Spoletan faction, in early 897 he had Formosus's body exhumed, placed on trial, stripped of its vestments and thrown into the Tiber, and his acts annulled. The outrage turned Rome against him: he was deposed, imprisoned and strangled in the summer of 897.

people.short_bio: Born at Gallese, son of Constantine, pope for about four months in 897. He was probably deposed and made a monk.
people.long_bio: Romanus, cardinal-priest of San Pietro in Vincoli, was elected after the fall of Stephen VI. His few known acts include granting the pallium to the patriarch of Grado and confirming the possessions of the Spanish sees of Elna and Gerona. He was deposed in November 897, probably by a rival faction, and seems to have ended his life as a monk.

notes: Rows 77-114 complete (38 people). Feast days checked against Vatican News saint-of-the-day pages (current calendar) where available; Catholic Encyclopedia feasts that differ (older Martyrology) are noted. Roster discrepancy: Leo IV consecration 10.V.847 in roster vs 10.IV.847 in Vatican Italian table and CE. Formosus: roster 'Bishop of Portus' is an office; birthplace set to Rome (probable, Treccani/CE). Sergius I: roster 'Syria' is family origin; Treccani gives birth at Palermo (set exact). Zachary: Vatican 'Greek', CE says Greek family in Calabria, Treccani says birthplace unknown; kept region Greece with public_note. Conon: unknown. John V: region Antioch (Treccani). Adrian III: cult confirmed 2 June 1891; feast 8 July (Treccani) vs 7 Sept (CE). Leo III: CE dates his 'canonization' to 1673 (Martyrology insertion); recorded as pre_congregation with that date. Adrian II birth year left null (c. 792 in some references, unverified). Formosus coordinates use precision 'exact' at Rome with 'probably' public note; integrator may prefer a flag.
